claims.text: Applying a sputter-deposited CrN coating to a boride-based component will significantly reduce molten-aluminum corrosion relative to an uncoated boride substrate.
A sputter-deposited CrN coating will form an adherent diffusion-barrier layer on a boride-based substrate.
A thin Cr buffer layer can improve adhesion of the CrN coating to the boride component.
Sputtering can produce a uniform and stable protective layer.
Exposure at 660–700 °C represents molten-aluminum conditions near aluminum's melting point.
Exposure for several tens of hours is representative of hot-dip aluminum-plating process cycles.
An inert or controlled atmosphere adequately mimics relevant aluminum-plating exposure conditions.
CrN is chemically inert under the proposed molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
A continuous, adherent CrN layer will limit interdiffusion and direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride matrix.
The CrN layer will inhibit dissolution and interfacial reactions of the boride substrate with molten aluminum.
Minimizing aluminum penetration into the component will slow the kinetics of corrosive degradation.
CrN-coated boride components will show lower corrosion rate, reduced weight loss, and less corrosion-product formation than uncoated components.
The reduced corrosion rate will improve component longevity in molten-aluminum environments.
The CrN coating will remain protective up to approximately 700 °C for durations typical of plating operations, provided it remains intact and adherent.
Spallation or cracking of the CrN coating will limit its protective performance.
The magnitude of corrosion-rate reduction will depend on coating thickness, deposition quality, and molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
Coating integrity may require further optimization under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses.
